Hire
hire
n. (wages due for work done; rendering Hebrew sakar, Greek misthos)
Old English hyr, wages. The biblical usage is almost entirely about timing and justice — not what a wage is but when it must be paid, and what happens when it is withheld.

Biblical Definition

A hire is wages earned, and Scripture's legislation about it is unusually urgent. The law requires same-day payment for the day labourer, and states the reason in human terms: “At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee” (Deuteronomy 24:15). The man is counting on that money for the evening meal; the employer who holds it overnight for his own convenience has taken food from a household, and the transaction is placed under God's ear. James takes up the same law against wealthy Christians and makes the wages themselves the plaintiff: “the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” (James 5:4) — unpaid wages cry out like Abel's blood. On the other side, the Lord Jesus establishes that gospel labour is real labour deserving real pay: “the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luke 10:7), and Paul cites that saying as scripture alongside Deuteronomy's unmuzzled ox (1 Timothy 5:18) — an early and remarkable indication that the Gospel words of Christ were already reckoned canonical.

Webster 1828 Definition

Wages due. The law requires the day labourer paid before sundown because he is counting on it; James says withheld wages cry into God's ears; and Christ establishes that the gospel labourer is worthy of his hire.

expand to see more

HIRE, v.t. [Sax. hyran.] To procure from another person and for temporary use, at a certain price, or for a stipulated or reasonable equivalent.

2. To engage in service for a stipulated reward; to contract with for a compensation; as, to hire a servant for a year.

HIRE, n. Wages; the price, reward or compensation paid or contracted to be given for the temporary use of a thing.

3. The reward or recompense paid for personal service. The laborer is worthy of his hire. Luke 10.

HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages; and hence, a mercenary, one who serves for reward only.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 24:15 — "At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee."

James 5:4 — "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."

Luke 10:7 — "And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house."

1 Timothy 5:18 — "For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward."

Modern Corruption

Luke 10:7 is stretched into a warrant for ministerial luxury, while the far more frequent biblical concern — wages withheld from working people — is treated as social commentary outside the church's proper business.

expand to see more

“The labourer is worthy of his hire” establishes a real and often neglected duty: churches ought to pay their ministers, and a congregation that keeps its pastor poor to keep him humble has misread both the text and human nature. Paul insists on the principle in 1 Corinthians 9 at length. But he insists on it while declining to use it, that he might make the gospel without charge, and he lists among an elder's qualifications that he be not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Timothy 3:3). The verse warrants a living, not an estate; and Peter's charge to feed the flock not for filthy lucre but of a ready mind (1 Peter 5:2) stands over every ministry whose finances would embarrass it if published. The Lord's own instruction in Luke 10 is notably modest — eat what is set before you, and do not shop for a better house.

The neglected half is the one Scripture presses hardest. Deuteronomy 24:15 and James 5:4 are about employers, and James is writing to a church. The sin named is not merely underpaying but delaying — keeping back what is owed, which in a day-labour economy meant a family went hungry that night, and which in a modern economy has its exact equivalents in slow payment to small contractors, misclassified workers, and wage theft that is cheaper to commit than to litigate. Scripture puts these cries in the ears of the Lord of sabaoth, the LORD of armies, which is a deliberately military title for a verse about payroll. A church that examines its members on doctrine and never on how they pay the people who work for them has an incomplete idea of what sin is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sakar (wages, hire) and sakir (a hired servant); Greek misthos (wages, reward) and misthios / misthotos (a hired servant, hireling).

expand to see more

Hebrew sakar (H7939) — wages, hire, reward; the word in Deuteronomy 24:15 and Genesis 15:1 (thy exceeding great reward).

Hebrew sakir (H7916) — a hired servant, day labourer; the class the law protects in Deuteronomy 24:14.

Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, hire, reward; the word in Luke 10:7 and James 5:4.

Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hireling; the man in John 10:12-13 who flees because the sheep are not his own.

Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, keep back by fraud; the verb in James 5:4.

Usage

"“Neither shall the sun go down upon it” — the day labourer is paid the same day, because he is counting on it."

"“The hire of the labourers… crieth” — withheld wages are a plaintiff before the Lord of sabaoth."

"“The labourer is worthy of his hire” — cited by Paul as scripture, alongside Deuteronomy."
